aspects.says: An ArrayList grows only when its array is full, to old + (old >> 1), and new ArrayList<>() allocates its default 10 slots on the first add.
basis: section:6.5.4.3. Capacity Considerations in Other Collections

aspects.says: HashMap spreads a hash with h ^ (h >>> 16) and takes its bucket as hash & (capacity - 1), so after doubling each entry stays or moves up by the old capacity.
basis: section:6.5.4.2. Resizing and Rehashing in HashMap

aspects.says: Since Java 8, ConcurrentHashMap's concurrencyLevel only raises the initial capacity to at least that value, and pre-sizing goes through initialCapacity.
ConcurrentHashMap resizes cooperatively: threads that find a resize in progress help migrate bins.
aspects.reason: internal mechanics invisible through the API and not deterministic to observe

aspects.says: A CopyOnWriteArrayList has no spare capacity: every add allocates an array one element longer.
basis: section:6.5.4.3. Capacity Considerations in Other Collections
aspects.reason: the internal array is not visible through the API; the copy-on-write cost itself is covered on page 6.5.1

aspects.says: A negative capacity, or a load factor of zero or less, throws IllegalArgumentException.
aspects.reason: argument checks of the constructors, minor and not practised

aspects.says: HashMap.newHashMap(n), HashSet.newHashSet(n) and LinkedHashMap.newLinkedHashMap(n) (Java 19+) pre-size for n mappings.
aspects.reason: a factory that does the resizes practice's calculation for the reader; the table size it picks is not visible through the Map API

aspects.says: A load factor above 1 is valid: the map holds more entries than buckets before it resizes, trading longer collision chains for less memory.
The default load factor 0.75 balances wasted space against collisions.
aspects.reason: a space and time trade-off no test can observe; the load factor's role as the resize trigger is practised in resizes, and a load factor above 1 is asked in the quiz

aspects.says: HashSet follows HashMap's capacity rules, and LinkedList has no capacity at all.
basis: section:6.5.4.3. Capacity Considerations in Other Collections
aspects.reason: incidental facts that follow from how each class is built; not practised

aspects.says: HashMap rounds a requested capacity up to the nearest power of two.
basis: section:6.5.4.1. Initial Capacity and Load Factor in HashMap

aspects.says: To hold n entries with no resize a HashMap is requested with (int) (n / 0.75f) + 1, since new HashMap<>(n) still resizes before n entries.
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

aspects.says: A resize is O(n): every entry is rehashed into the new table.
basis: section:6.5.4.2. Resizing and Rehashing in HashMap
aspects.reason: a cost claim no deterministic test can observe; how often resizes happen is what the resizes practice counts

aspects.says: A HashMap doubles its table when its size goes above capacity * loadFactor, which is 7 resizes on the way to 1000 entries from the defaults.
basis: section:6.5.4.2. Resizing and Rehashing in HashMap

aspects.says: ArrayList.trimToSize shrinks the array to the size, and ensureCapacity pre-allocates before a bulk insert.
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them
aspects.reason: an ArrayList's array length is not visible through its API, so no test can tell whether trimToSize or ensureCapacity was called; the growth practice models the lengths instead
